title: Good Leaders Explain How Failure Will Be Judged Before It Happens https://admiredleadership.com/good-leaders-explain-how-failure-will-be-judged-before-it-happens/
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The piece argues that resilient teams are distinguished not by avoiding failure but by knowing in advance exactly how failure will be judged, and that most leaders fail their teams by only revealing their evaluation standards after something has already gone wrong. It proposes a specific, advance-stated framework built around process integrity, prompt disclosure, and willingness to ask for help, rather than outcome alone, as the true criteria good leaders should communicate before failure occurs. The author argues that when leaders skip this step, teams manage the appearance of success rather than its substance, because nobody knows what will actually be forgiven versus punished, and a single unrepresentative incident becomes the team's only data point about the leader's real standards. The piece closes on a paradox: telling people in advance how failure will be judged actually reduces the frequency and severity of failure, because it makes concealment, not failure itself, the behavior people learn to avoid.
points: Argues the key leadership failure is not that failure happens but that the criteria for judging it are only revealed after the fact, making standards look arbitrary or political.
Proposes a concrete pre-stated evaluation framework: did the person follow a sound process, disclose the problem promptly, and ask for help, rather than judging purely on outcome.
Warns that a team with no advance framing learns their leader's true standards from a single incident, which then colors every subsequent failure through that one unrepresentative data point.

Identifies a paradox: explicitly telling people in advance how failure will be judged reduces the frequency and severity of failure, because it rewards surfacing problems early rather than hiding them.
quotes: What separates resilient teams from fragile ones is not whether failure happens, but whether people understand, in advance, how that failure will be evaluated.

When the criteria for judging failure only become visible after the fact, people reasonably conclude that the standard is arbitrary, or worse, that it will be applied punitively depending on politics or mood.
A team that has never been told how failure will be judged learns, from a single incident, exactly one data point about their leader's true standards. That is a dangerous way to build trust.
If you follow the agreed process, disclose problems immediately, and ask for help when you need it, a bad outcome will not define how I see you.

People stop hiding problems because they know concealment, not failure itself, is what will actually be punished. They start asking for help earlier because they know that asking is rewarded, not treated as an admission of weakness.

The paradox is that clarifying how failure will be judged, before it happens, is one of the most effective ways to reduce the frequency and severity of failure itself, because it makes the early warning signs of failure something people surface rather than hide.
